chunks: "There are a few standard grades. Commercial parts are usually specified from 0 to 70 degrees C. Industrial is minus 40 to 85.
Automotive follows AEC-Q100 grades: Grade 3 is minus 40 to 85, Grade 2 is minus 40 to 105, Grade 1 is minus 40 to 125, and Grade 0 goes up to 150 degrees ambient.
Military and space parts typically use minus 55 to 125. Those are the ambient or case ranges a part is guaranteed to work in.
The thing to keep straight is that validation cares about junction temperature, which is higher than ambient: T j equals T a plus P theta JA .
A chip dissipating 2 watts with 30 K per watt thermal resistance at 85 C ambient is at 145 C junction, past a 125 C limit, so the thermal solution matters as much as the silicon.
In validation I'd test at the cold end, a room temperature point, and the hot end, across supply voltage extremes and process corners.
Cold finds timing and startup problems, like slow-at-cold behavior from temperature inversion, analog drift, and cold boot.
Hot finds leakage-driven power and thermal limits, setup failures in older nodes, and reliability.
On top of that, qualification runs reliability tests like temperature cycling and high-temperature operating life at 125 C or more.
And these numbers aren't universal; the actual range depends on the product's market and the company's spec."
